lesson.title: Fighting Back with Capacitors: Leading Power Factor
lesson.summary: Capacitive reactance makes current lead voltage, producing a leading power factor that can be used deliberately to cancel out an inductive load's lagging power factor.
lesson.body:
Every inductive load, motors, transformers, fluorescent ballasts, pulls current that lags voltage, producing a lagging power factor and forcing the source to carry more current than the real power alone would require. Capacitive reactance does the mathematical opposite: it makes current lead voltage. A circuit dominated by capacitance, or an inductive circuit with enough capacitance deliberately added, has a negative impedance angle and, correspondingly, a leading power factor, current arriving ahead of voltage in each cycle rather than behind it.

Swap the running example's inductor for a capacitor of equal reactance to see this concretely: R = 30 Ω and XC = 40 Ω in series, giving Z = 30 − j40 Ω = 50∠−53.13° Ω, magnitude unchanged from the earlier inductive case, only the sign of the angle flips. Driven by the same V = 120∠0° V rms source, I = V/Z = 120∠0° / 50∠−53.13° = 2.4∠53.13° A: the current phasor now sits above the real axis instead of below it, meaning current leads voltage by 53.13°.

Average power depends on cos θ, unchanged by the sign flip since cosine is an even function: P = 120 × 2.4 × cos(53.13°) = 288 × 0.6000 = 172.8 W, identical to the inductive case. Reactive power, however, depends on sin θ, an odd function, so its sign flips: Q = 120 × 2.4 × sin(−53.13°) = 288 × (−0.8000) = −230.4 VAR, negative by convention to signal that the load is capacitive rather than inductive. The power factor magnitude is still pf = cos(53.13°) = 0.6, but it is now reported as 0.6 leading.

This sign convention is exactly what makes power factor correction possible: a lagging inductive load and a leading capacitive load, placed in parallel, draw reactive power of opposite sign, so the reactive components partially cancel while both continue to draw whatever real power they individually need. A factory motor load at 0.6 lagging can have capacitor banks added in parallel, sized specifically to supply a matching leading reactive power, pushing the combined power factor of the whole installation back up toward 1.0 without changing how much real work the motors do.

The same geometric shortcut used for lagging power factor applies here too: cos θ = R/|Z| = 30/50 = 0.6000, unchanged, since flipping the sign of X flips θ but not R or |Z|. In practice, power factor correction has to be sized carefully: adding too much capacitance can overcorrect a lagging load into a net leading power factor, which some utilities penalize just as they penalize a lagging one, so the goal is usually to bring the combined power factor close to 1.0 rather than push it as far as possible in the leading direction. This is the payoff of the entire phasor framework built up through this chapter: representing sinusoidal voltages and currents as complex numbers turns a subtle physical timing relationship, whether current arrives early or late relative to voltage, into a simple sign that can be read off, added, and engineered against directly.
